<reason>The debate turned on whether cutting access to capped-rate cards actually protects vulnerable borrowers or merely reroutes them to worse, unregulated credit (payday, title loans). A opened with vivid moral framing and a coherent underwriting story, but its key defensive move — "fringe lenders already coexist with uncapped cards, so a cap changes nothing" — was directly and correctly undercut by B's point that existing fringe-market size reflects an already-excluded population, while a binding cap adds *new marginal* borrowers to that pool, a distinction A never squarely answered. Instead of repairing that mechanism, A pivoted to a burden-shift ("you must prove they land worse"), which is a legitimate rhetorical move given the motion's wording, but it never demonstrated that the benefit to remaining borrowers actually outweighs the substitution harm — it mostly asserted the trade was worth it. B also landed a sharper strategic blow by pointing out that the sympathetic "broken car, medical bill" borrower from A's own opening is precisely the population most likely to be excluded and pushed toward worse credit, turning A's central example against itself. A's answers to pressure questions were competent but largely reframing rather than resolving; B's answers, despite being followed by two clipped speeches (a real execution cost), more directly engaged the mechanism in dispute and left the crucial substitution claim less damaged.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's identification of the "marginal borrower" flaw in A's coexistence argument ([B2.3]-[B2.4]), reinforced by turning A's own "broken car/medical bill" example against them in the closing ([B5.2]), was the most decisive exchange; A never fully repaired this and retreated to a burden-shift instead of rebutting the mechanism directly.</best_rebuttal>
